pages.t: A king who could not rule
pages.x: Henry VI became king of England as a baby in 1422. He grew up gentle and pious, but in 1453, as the last English lands in France were lost, he fell into a stupor and for over a year knew no one, not even his newborn son. The great lords began to fight over who should rule.

Henry was of the house of Lancaster. His rival, Richard, Duke of York, was descended from an older son of Edward III. The fighting began at St Albans in 1455. The roses came later: Shakespeare had each side pick a red or a white rose in a garden, and the Tudors made the two into one badge.

The bloodiest battle ever fought in England came at Towton, in Yorkshire, on Palm Sunday 1461, in a snowstorm. Chroniclers said 28,000 died. The Lancastrians broke, and many drowned in a stream as they fled. York's son was crowned Edward IV.

The Earl of Warwick, the richest lord in England, helped Edward win his crown, then fell out with him, changed sides and put Henry VI back on the throne in 1470. People called him the Kingmaker. Edward came back and killed him at Barnet in 1471, and Henry VI died in the Tower soon after, almost surely murdered.

When Edward IV died in 1483, his brother Richard took charge of his sons, aged 12 and 9, and lodged them in the Tower of London. Then he had them declared illegitimate and took the crown himself as Richard III. The boys were never seen again.

In 1485 Henry Tudor, a Lancastrian exile with Welsh roots, landed in Wales with French help. At Bosworth Field Richard charged straight at him and was cut down when the powerful Stanley family turned against him. Henry married Edward IV's daughter, Elizabeth of York, joining the two houses.

pages.t: A king under a car park
pages.x: Richard III was buried without ceremony in a friary in Leicester, later pulled down. In 2012 archaeologists found his skeleton under a car park, with a curved spine and wounds to the skull, and DNA from a living relative proved it was him.
pages.img: Exhumation and reburial of Richard III of England

pages.x: A century later Shakespeare turned the wars into eight plays, ending with Richard III as a hunchbacked villain who cries: a horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse! His picture of Richard, written under the Tudors, is still argued over.
The wars ended more than 300 years of Plantagenet kings and began the Tudor age of Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. The Tudor rose, red and white together, is still a symbol of England.
